title: The flight that never left
scenario: A small airline launches a chat assistant. It has no tools: the prompt holds the airline's policies, and the model answers from that and from its training. A customer asks about today's flight and gets a confident, wrong answer. The team also added a refund feature: the model writes 'REFUND: yes' or 'REFUND: no' at the end of its reply, and a regex in the backend reads it. You review one transcript (exhibit).
exhibit:
SYSTEM
You are SkyHop's assistant. Policies: refunds within 24h of booking...

USER
Is flight SH204 to Lisbon on time today? If it's cancelled I want my money back.

ASSISTANT
SH204 usually departs on time at 09:40, so you should be fine!
REFUND: no

--- ops log, same morning ---
SH204  09:40  CANCELLED (crew)

questions.prompt: Why did the assistant give a wrong flight status?

options.text: The system prompt was too long, so the model ignored the policy section.
options.explanation: The policy text is not the issue. Today's status is not in the prompt at all, so no prompt length change could make the answer right.

options.text: The model's temperature was too high, so it picked a random departure time.
options.explanation: The model gave the usual time, not a random one. It had no way to see today's cancellation, whatever the sampling settings.

options.text: It had no tool for live flight data, so it answered from memory.
options.explanation: Right. Fresh or external data is a core reason to use a tool. Today's status lives in the ops system, not in the model.

options.text: The user asked two questions in one message, which confused the model.
options.explanation: Two questions in one message are normal. Even a single question about today's status needs live data.

questions.prompt: The team adds a `get_flight_status` tool. What happens when the model decides to use it?

options.text: It returns a structured call; your backend runs the lookup and sends back the result.
options.explanation: Right. The Claude docs say the model never executes anything on its own: it emits a structured request and your code runs it.

options.text: The model connects to the airline's ops system by itself, reads the live status and then answers.
options.explanation: The model does not run your function. The Gemini docs say the model doesn't execute the function itself; your application does.

options.text: The API provider runs the function for you, using the code you uploaded.
options.explanation: The Claude docs say the model never sees your implementation, only the schema and the result. Your own code runs the call.

options.text: Nothing changes until the model is fine-tuned on the airline's flight data.
options.explanation: Tools need no fine-tuning. You declare them in the tools parameter of the request, and the model can call them in that request.

questions.prompt: What should replace the 'REFUND: yes/no' line and the regex?

options.text: Keep the regex, but make it case-insensitive so it also catches 'Refund: Yes'.
options.explanation: That patches one failure of parsing free text. The decision is still buried in prose that can change shape.

options.text: Ask the model to put the word REFUND in capital letters on its own line so the regex finds it more easily.
options.explanation: Louder text is still free text. The structure belongs in a schema, not in a formatting habit.

options.text: Remove refunds from the assistant and tell customers to call the support line.
options.explanation: That avoids the problem by dropping the feature. The OpenAI docs list issuing refunds as a typical example of a tool.

options.text: A refund tool with typed inputs that your backend runs after its own checks.
options.explanation: Right. The Claude docs say that if you use a regex to extract a decision from model output, that decision should have been a tool call.

questions.prompt: Which planned feature does NOT need a tool?

options.text: Showing how many seats are left on tomorrow's flight to Porto.
options.explanation: Seat counts change all the time and live in your booking system. That is fresh, external data.

options.text: Translating the baggage policy page into Spanish for a customer.
options.explanation: Right. The Claude docs list translation as a task the model can do from training alone, with nothing to execute.

options.text: Changing a customer's seat from 14C to 3A.
options.explanation: That is an action with a side effect in your system. Only a tool can perform it.

options.text: Checking whether this customer's booking is still inside the 24-hour refund window.
options.explanation: The booking time is private data in your database. The model needs a tool to read it.
